questions.question: What command initializes a new Git repository?
questions.explanation: git init creates a hidden .git directory in the current folder, initializing an empty Git repository.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the Git workflow?
questions.explanation: The Git workflow is: edit files → git add (stage) → git commit (save snapshot) → git push (send to remote).

questions.question: What does 'git add .' do?
options: Stages all modified and new files in the current directory
questions.correct_answer: Stages all modified and new files in the current directory
questions.explanation: git add . stages all changes (modified and new files) in the current directory and subdirectories for the next commit.

questions.question: What is the Staging Area in Git?
options: A temporary area where you prepare changes before committing
questions.correct_answer: A temporary area where you prepare changes before committing
questions.explanation: The staging area (index) lets you choose exactly which changes to include in the next commit, giving fine-grained control.

questions.question: What does git checkout -b feature/login do?
options: Creates and switches to a new branch named feature/login
questions.correct_answer: Creates and switches to a new branch named feature/login
questions.explanation: The -b flag creates a new branch and immediately switches to it, combining git branch and git checkout into one command.

questions.question: When does a merge conflict occur?
options: Any time you merge two branches
When the same lines are changed differently in both branches being merged
When a branch is behind main
When there are too many commits
questions.correct_answer: When the same lines are changed differently in both branches being merged
questions.explanation: Git auto-merges changes in different parts of files. Conflicts occur only when the exact same lines were modified in both branches.

questions.question: Which command safely undoes a commit on a shared branch without rewriting history?
questions.explanation: git revert creates a new commit that reverses previous changes, preserving history — safe for branches that others are working on.

questions.question: What does git stash do?
options: Commits all changes without a message
Temporarily saves uncommitted changes so you can switch branches
questions.correct_answer: Temporarily saves uncommitted changes so you can switch branches
questions.explanation: git stash saves your working directory changes temporarily. git stash pop restores them when you're ready to continue.

questions.question: What files should always be in .gitignore?
questions.explanation: node_modules/ is huge and reproducible from package.json. .env contains secrets. Neither should ever be committed to version control.

questions.question: What is the conventional commit prefix for a new feature?
questions.explanation: Conventional Commits specification uses 'feat:' for new features, 'fix:' for bug fixes, 'docs:' for documentation, etc.

questions.question: What does HEAD point to in Git?
options: The current active branch or commit
questions.correct_answer: The current active branch or commit
questions.explanation: HEAD is a special pointer to your current position in the repository — usually the tip of the active branch.

questions.question: What does git log --oneline show?
options: A compact one-line summary of each commit
questions.correct_answer: A compact one-line summary of each commit
questions.explanation: --oneline condenses each commit to one line showing the short hash and commit message, making history easy to scan.

questions.question: What is the difference between git reset --soft and git reset --hard?
options: --soft keeps changes staged; --hard discards all changes
--soft is for branches; --hard is for files
questions.correct_answer: --soft keeps changes staged; --hard discards all changes
questions.explanation: --soft undoes the commit but keeps changes staged. --hard undoes the commit AND permanently discards all changes (use with caution).

questions.question: What does git remote add origin <url> do?
options: Creates a new repository on GitHub
Links your local repo to a remote repository URL
questions.correct_answer: Links your local repo to a remote repository URL
questions.explanation: 'origin' is the conventional name for your main remote. This command establishes the connection between local and remote repos.

questions.question: What does git pull do?
options: Downloads remote changes and merges them into current branch
Creates a new branch from remote
questions.correct_answer: Downloads remote changes and merges them into current branch
questions.explanation: git pull is equivalent to git fetch (download) + git merge (integrate) — it brings remote changes into your current local branch.
